request: Exposure disagrees with the policy dates.
evidence: About 1 row in 175 disagrees with its own dates: some written in days, some on a 360-day year. Declared exposure is 35% above the exposure implied by the dates. The test has no such rows.
alternative: Use the declared exposure as given.
decision: Recompute exposure from the dates for every row that is off by more than half a day.
effect: The largest single fix: the motor model loses 0.154 → 0.112 D² on the 2024 fold without it.

request: Sums insured appear in two units.
evidence: Sum insured per bedroom forms two clusters exactly three orders of magnitude apart, in train and test; nothing lies between them.
alternative: Leave it to the trees, which put the large values in the top class anyway.
decision: Divide by 1,000 when the value per bedroom exceeds 100× the median.
effect: Small but positive (about +0.0007 D² on contents).

request: Some claims cannot belong to any policy row.
evidence: 598 exact duplicates (only the claim id differs), 270 claims in 2020, 139 before inception, 1,711 repudiated. The claim table has no row id: each claim is placed by policy and date.
alternative: Keep all claims.
decision: Remove them; every remaining claim falls in exactly one row. Reconciliation raw − excluded = valid is checked in code.
effect: 163,150 → 160,432 valid claims.

request: Reconstruct how the data were generated before choosing a model.
evidence: For each of 15 perils, an additive frequency model (one split per tree) against one with interactions: additive is as good or better in 14 of 15 (only subsidence = soil × drought interacts). Severity is nearly flat with a few drivers. About 30 columns have no effect.
alternative: A large generic model on all columns.
decision: Frequency × severity per peril, additive, with a short list of severity drivers; the decoy columns are excluded.
effect: Public +0.0012 (sub_03); the local Qwen loop later found the same decoys on its own.

request: Check whether customer-service contacts reveal claims not yet reported.
evidence: Rows with 0 / 1 / 2 claims average 0.50 / 3.2 / 5.8 contacts, so contacts are generated by claims. In the 2025 test they sit at the no-claim level (0.51; maximum 6 against 36 in training).
alternative: Use contacts as a rating factor.
decision: Excluded as a feature (leakage). Used only to add expected late-reported claims to each motor policy's 2024 history.
effect: History completion passes on all judges for motor (+0.34 / +0.39 e-4) and fails for home; kept for motor only (sub_50).

request: Keep all years in one database and test a year flag.
evidence: 2025 is a value the model never saw: a tree treats it as 2024, a GLM turns it into a trend already handled by the offset. Year weights made the folds worse.
alternative: Year as a variable, or one model per year.
decision: One model on 2021–24; what changes between years enters through variables known in 2025 (weather, ages, tenure) and the per-peril trend.
effect: No extrapolation outside the fitted range.

request: Observed reporting delays are right-truncated at 31/12/2024.
evidence: Counting observed delays at 31/12/2024 under-states them: recent bodily-injury claims are missing. A reverse-time estimator for right-truncated data looks at each delay only in the years it could have been seen.
alternative: Empirical delay distribution.
decision: Reverse-time estimator per peril; each row gets a completeness π (share of its claims already reported).
effect: A 2024 motor row has seen about 57% of its bodily-injury claims; later backtested on Part 2 data (actual/predicted 0.97–1.07).

request: Verify with numbers that IBNR and trend are needed for a two-year horizon.
evidence: Without development the 2024 motor year costs 448 per exposure year instead of 574: it would look like the cheapest year only because it is the youngest, and the model would learn that recent policies cost less.
alternative: Use reported cost as the target.
decision: Keep IBNR and IBNER; apply trend only where the data measure it.
effect: Motor level about 10% higher than with reported cost; a flat cost by origin year once on the 2025 level.

request: Re-estimate the bodily-injury severity trend on its own data instead of borrowing the line median.
evidence: Bodily-injury severity has no significant trend of its own (+1.9% a year in the 18 October data, −1.2% in the final pipeline); the rule gave it the 8.0% of short-tail perils. With the borrowed trend the 2025 level falls by origin year (659 → 626), a sign of over-trending; with its own estimate it is flat (591–610).
alternative: Borrow the median of significant perils.
decision: Each peril keeps its own severity trend estimate; the IBNER inflation of bodily injury is set to 1.9%.
effect: Motor level 632 → 593 per exposure year; public +0.0005 (sub_16).

request: One claim dominates the motor excess.
evidence: An open 2023 bodily-injury claim of 11.9 million is alone 55% of all motor excess. Large claims follow the predicted frequency of their peril, but a frequency-proportional load is not measurable on the score (27 events).
alternative: No cap, or a risk-proportional large-loss load.
decision: Cap at 150k / 250k / 50k (about the 99.9th percentile) and spread the excess as a flat load per exposure year.
effect: Stable levels; the proportional load was tested and dropped.

request: The official validation target spreads IBNR over all rows.
evidence: The official target spreads IBNR uniformly over all rows: 22% of the 2024 motor target sits on rows regardless of claims, which rewards flatter predictions and explained a failed submission.
alternative: Judge only on the official target.
decision: Three judges: official (imitates Kaggle), own (reported cost against prediction × completeness, decides the shape), true large losses.
effect: Every later change was kept only if it improved both years on official and own.

request: Test IBNR allocated only to rows with claims against spread IBNR.
evidence: 80% of late-reported claims arrive on rows without a reported claim; rows with a claim have a lift of 1.33 at equal prediction.
alternative: IBNR only on rows with claims.
decision: The frequency model uses reported counts with offset log(exposure × π); IBNR stays spread only in the official judge.
effect: No artificial concentration of IBNR.

request: Quantify how much of the error is reducible before adding complexity.
evidence: Tweedie deviance is a Bregman divergence: error = noise + distance to the true mean. A simulation calibrated on our data gives 82.8% noise, 4.3% unseen policy risk, 12.7% rating factors, 0.2% history.
alternative: Keep adding model complexity.
decision: Stop chasing gains below the noise; spend effort on the target and on policy history.
effect: Our out-of-sample 0.1290 matches 0.1285 ± 0.002 for a perfect model with the same information.

request: Residuals of the same policy correlate across years.
evidence: Residual counts of the same policy correlate between 2023 and 2024: a multiplicative policy effect with variance φ ≈ 0.43 (motor).
alternative: Rating factors only.
decision: Experience rating, Bühlmann–Straub: factor = (N + k) / (E + k) on the policy's own history.
effect: Public +0.0025 (sub_05), the largest single step.

request: Compare GLM and GBM peril by peril on equal terms.
evidence: Same variables and offset: the Poisson GLM loses in 28 of 30 peril × fold cases (flood by −0.02). A one-split GBM is already additive like a GLM but chooses thresholds from the data.
alternative: GLM for some perils.
decision: GBM stumps for frequency everywhere; GLM kept for severity only where it wins both years.
effect: Confirmed the structure; contents flood severity mix tested on the leaderboard and within noise.

request: Set the rule: no post-hoc transforms of predictions.
evidence: A power calibration pred^b that won on our folds lost 0.00035 on the public leaderboard (sub_21): it was fitted on models with fewer years.
alternative: Post-hoc multipliers or powers.
decision: Rule: change the model or an assumption, never the predictions afterwards.
effect: Level probes became diagnostics only.

request: Model the deductible as gross-then-net and test it.
evidence: Claim amounts carry no trace of the deductible (same severity with 0 or 1,000 voluntary excess); frequency falls with it and the effect fades with the insured value (interaction z = 4.6).
alternative: Net the deductible from a gross amount.
decision: Relative deductible (deductible ÷ value) in motor own-damage and theft frequency and in the buildings GBM; checked against four random control columns.
effect: +0.00025 / +0.00008 on buildings, above the noise columns (sub_48).

request: Decide motor credibility with the official judge, the frozen holdout and the public board together.
evidence: Paired bootstrap: official judge +4.5 e-4 (P = 0.95) for k = 16, own judge −2.8 (P = 0.05). The frozen 10% holdout and the public board side with the official judge.
alternative: Keep k = 8 by the both-judges rule.
decision: k = 16 for motor; the disagreement is recorded.
effect: Final Part 1 submission sub_51: private 0.13875, 2nd of 51.

request: The automated audit lists what changed in the new market.
evidence: Two policy years, new regions, gender, ages only in bands, no credit band, mileage or telematics, 3.5× the wildfire index, and a 2025 book that is 76% new business from a broker.
alternative: Run the Part 1 pipeline unchanged.
decision: One configuration file: harmonised age bands, construction-code map, region dropped from the prior, development borrowed.
effect: The same pipeline ran on the new market in one step.

request: Reporting delays look the same in both markets.
evidence: Reporting delays match per peril (bodily injury: 86% reported within a year in both). Backtest: accident year 2023 seen at end-2023, developed with Part 1 curves, predicts end-2024 counts within 0.97–1.07 on every peril.
alternative: Estimate development on two years of data.
decision: Borrow reporting curves, IBNER and trends from Part 1.
effect: Two years give no degrees of freedom for a trend; the borrowed one is tested instead.

request: Use the Part 1 model as prior and measure how far the emerging data can move it.
evidence: Fit 2023 → score 2024 (D²): emerging data only 0.131 / 0.025 / 0.061; Part 1 prior × emerging level 0.146 / 0.085 / 0.118. A simulation of a small market inside the developed one agrees in 16 of 18 cases.
alternative: A model built only on the new data.
decision: Part 1 model as prior; the emerging data set the level and only the corrections they can support.
effect: Wins on every line.

request: Fix the decision rule before testing; use the public board only as a check.
evidence: Our own public-vs-private pairs from Part 1: public gaps below 0.0005 were coin flips on the private board.
alternative: Follow the public board.
decision: A seven-check bench fixed in advance (two time splits, five policy groups); a correction is kept if it wins at least 5 of 7 on both the shape and the own judge.
effect: Broad corrections (GBM, 19-variable GLM) failed; three targeted corrections passed.

request: Check whether the acquired broker portfolio is worse than organic business, by peril and policy age.
evidence: New business costs 19% more than renewals (bootstrap CI 0–41%). Frequency is at par (0.91–1.08); the excess is severity from five bodily-injury claims; without them actual/expected is 0.97.
alternative: Ignore new business, or cap the correction.
decision: Keep the credibility-weighted new-business correction and state its uncertainty in the report.
effect: Public 0.16472 with it, 0.16236 capped, 0.16100 without: consistent with the internal sign.

request: Test more credibility for the new data, including levels per peril.
evidence: Per-peril levels pass the bench only for contents (credibility k 100/200); for motor and buildings they lose.
alternative: Per-peril levels on every line.
decision: Per-peril level for contents only.
effect: Part of the final p2_sub_10.

request: Test one pooled model with a market flag, also with a GBM.
evidence: Pooled additive model with a market flag: worse on motor and buildings, contents better in only 4 of 7 checks; with interactions worse everywhere.
alternative: Pooled model.
decision: Rejected; keep prior × emerging level.
effect: Recorded as a tested alternative.

request: Large claims occur at a different rate in the new market.
evidence: Large claims are rarer in the emerging motor book (0.35× the developed frequency above 30k) and more frequent in buildings (2.17× above 125k).
alternative: Copy the developed load.
decision: Developed Pareto tail (motor, threshold 50k, α 1.98) rescaled by the emerging/developed ratio of large-claim frequencies.
effect: Loads 5.0 / 11.2 / 0.37 per exposure year (p2_sub_10).

request: The buildings level is unstable at emerging size.
evidence: At emerging size the buildings level has a standard deviation of 16%; weighting the 2023 fire year moves it by ±25%.
alternative: Tune the level on the public board.
decision: State the uncertainty with its price effect; no tuning.
effect: Sensitivity table in the report.

request: Drop the variables that exist only in the old database and refit the same model.
evidence: Region, credit band, mileage and telematics exist only in Part 1; ages exist only in bands in Part 2.
alternative: Prior fitted on all Part 1 columns.
decision: Prior refitted on the developed data with the common columns only (region dropped, age bands harmonised).
effect: A prior the emerging data can actually use.

request: Have the local model review the pipeline code for leakage, bugs and Part 2 robustness.
evidence: The pipeline would soon run on a new market with other years, columns and units; nobody had read every file with that in mind.
alternative: Adapt the code only when Part 2 breaks it.
decision: The local model reviewed 25 code chunks through three lenses (leakage, bugs, Part 2 robustness), then tried to refute its own findings; the survivors were checked by hand.
effect: 125 findings, 93 refuted by Qwen itself, 7 true; no leakage; 4 fixes (hard-coded lines and mature years, missing-column guards) that the Part 2 market needed.

request: Check whether the broker portfolio looks like the new business the model was estimated on, and whether the model can be fitted on it.
evidence: A classifier on all rating variables cannot tell the 2025 broker policies from the emerging new business of 2023–24 (AUC 0.52–0.53). Expected cost under the prior: motor 760 against 787 per exposure year, buildings 580 against 588, contents 120 against 117. Both have 28% young drivers against 18% for renewals.
alternative: Fit or tune the model on the broker policies, or on the public third of the test.
decision: Keep the model and the new-business correction; no re-weighting, since the populations already match. The broker policies have no claims, so they cannot be a training or validation set.
effect: The new-business assumption rests on a portfolio that looks like the one it was estimated on; stated in the report.

request: Run autonomous AI experiments only under a frozen judge the agent cannot modify.
evidence: Karpathy-style loops: the local model edits one file; a frozen judge it cannot modify scores both validation years; guardrails refuse code that reads the validation target or imports modules.
alternative: Let the agent tune freely.
decision: A change is kept only if the worse year improves, then re-run on our three judges (Part 1) or the bench (Part 2) before entering a submission.
effect: 731 experiments in Part 1, 11 kept; one Qwen model in the Part 1 blend after the actuary found and fixed its wrong monotone constraint.
